What is necessary in order to use Dolt in a private Git repository that should never be pushed to GitHub as a backing for Beads (bd)?

Nothing about Dolt requires GitHub. For replication you configure a Dolt remote pointing at any Git remote whose URL is accepted as a Git-style remote (HTTPS or SSH to self-hosted GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo, a bare repo on disk (file://… or a path ending in .git), etc.). Dolt stores its sync payload under a Git ref (default refs/dolt/data). Dolt docs — Using Remotes (Git remotes)
What is necessary in order to use Dolt in a private Git repository that should never be pushed to GitHub as a backing for Beads (bd)?

Tooling prerequisites — Install dolt and ensure git is on your PATH (Dolt shells out to Git for Git remotes). The empty-repo caveat: the Git remote must already have at least one branch; initialize it with a seed commit before the first dolt push. Same section — Requirements and caveats
What is necessary in order to use Dolt in a private Git repository that should never be pushed to GitHub as a backing for Beads (bd)?

Private / never-on-GitHub — Use a non-GitHub URL when you run dolt remote add inside the Beads Dolt database directory (typically .beads/dolt/ after bd init). Examples from the docs: git+https://host/org/repo.git, git@host:org/repo.git, ../remote.git, or file:///abs/path/to/repo.git. Authentication is ordinary Git access (SSH keys, HTTPS credentials, etc.) to that host. Git remotes — Accepted URL formats
What is necessary in order to use Dolt in a private Git repository that should never be pushed to GitHub as a backing for Beads (bd)?

Beads-specific — bd keeps the live DB under .beads/dolt/ and sync is “Dolt-native”; configure remotes the same way you would for standalone Dolt, then use Beads’ Dolt commands (e.g. bd dolt …) per project docs. If CLI and the embedded server disagree on remotes, bd doctor --fix and issues around bd dolt pull vs dolt pull are documented in the tracker (remote config must live where both see it). Beads Quick Start — Database location

In : this page is filed here as a reminder to capture one portable story for Beads / [[bd]] across Agentic Engineering Tools, instead of re-deriving setup from each vendor doc every time.
Official docs describe per-IDE / per-agent wiring so agents know how to use bd (hooks, plugins, CLI setup, etc.). Beads — IDE setup is the hub for that.

This garden already uses [[rulesync]] as the single source for rules, commands, skills, and related AI-tool config that fans out to Claude/Code, CursorAI/CLI, Codex/CLI, Copilot-style targets, and the rest.

Gap: there is no rulesync-authored rule or skill yet that tells every tool the same baseline: this repo uses Beads; run these setup or registration steps for your runtime; keep issue state in sync the same way.
Points agents at bd when the repo has .beads/ (or documents how to detect “Beads project”).
Summarizes or links the IDE-setup matrix (what bd setup … exists, what needs a plugin, what is hook-only) without duplicating upstream forever.
Aligns with existing workflow rules—e.g. [[AI/Coding/Concept/Land the Plane]] / .rulesync landing-the-plane material that already expects agents to run bd sync before push where Beads is in use.

Optional stretch: a progressive-disclosure skill (see [[rulesync/How To/Write Skills With Progressive Disclosure]]) so lightweight installs only see a checklist, and deep references stay in references/.

A binary cache is a cache of already-built artifacts, so a system can download trusted build outputs instead of rebuilding the same derivations locally.

In Nix, binary caches are one of the practical levers that make reproducible builds usable day to day: CI can build once, publish the result, and developer machines or deploy targets can fetch the matching store paths later.
Cachix is centered on hosted Nix binary cache sharing.
DeterminateSystems offers binary-cache features through FlakeHub Cache.
BiomeJS is a comprehensive web development toolchain that combines formatting, linting, and code analysis into a single, fast tool
Built with Rust for performance, designed as a unified replacement for multiple tools like ESLint, Prettier, and other JavaScript tooling
Aims to be "one toolchain for your web project" with a focus on speed, simplicity, and scalability
JavaScript ecosystem traditionally requires multiple tools: ESLint for linting, Prettier for formatting, various plugins for different file types
Performance overhead from running separate processes
Maintenance burden of keeping tools compatible
BiomeJS emerged to consolidate these tools into a single, performant solution
Inspired by rust-analyzer's architecture for language tooling
Unified Toolchain - Single tool handles formatting, linting, and code analysis
Performance First - Built in Rust, approximately 35x faster than Prettier
Zero Configuration - Works out of the box with sensible defaults
Compatibility - 97% compatible with Prettier, includes 360+ rules from ESLint ecosystem
Scalability - Designed to handle projects of any size efficiently
Actionable Diagnostics - Provides detailed, contextual error messages
Built in Rust for native performance
Inspired by rust-analyzer's innovative language tooling approach
Can process multiple file types through unified API
Formatting: Reformats code to consistent style (97% Prettier-compatible)
Linting: Checks code against 360+ rules from ESLint and TypeScript ESLint
Check: Single command (biome check) runs all operations together
